question_text: The volume of drink dispensed by a coffee machine is normally distributed with mean 254 mL and standard deviation 2.3 mL.

subparts.stem: Find the probability that a randomly selected drink from the machine will have volume less than 254 mL.
subparts.solution:
Let the volume of a randomly selected drink be $X\text{ mL}$.
$X \sim \text{N}(254, (2.3)^2)$.
Since the normal distribution is symmetrical about the mean $\mu = 254$:
$$P(X < 254) = 0.5$$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The normal curve is symmetric about its mean, so exactly half the probability lies below the mean.
step_by_step: Observe that $X < 254$ represents the lower half of the distribution.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Performing unnecessary complicated numerical integration on GDC.

subparts.stem: Find the percentage of drinks dispensed by the machine which have volume between 252 mL and 256 mL.

mark_breakdown.desc: Setting up normal cumulative distribution $P(252 \le X \le 256)$ with $\mu = 254, \sigma = 2.3$

subparts.solution:
Using technology:
Lower: $252$, Upper: $256$, $\sigma = 2.3$, $\mu = 254$
$$P(252 \le X \le 256) \approx 0.615$$
$\therefore$ about $61.5\%$ of drinks dispensed by the machine have volume between $252\text{ mL}$ and $256\text{ mL}$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The probability that a normal variable lies in an interval $[a, b]$ is the area under the normal curve between $a$ and $b$.
step_by_step: Set lower bound to 252 and upper bound to 256.

subparts.stem: A sample of 80 drinks is taken from the machine. Determine the number of drinks which will be expected to have volume at least two standard deviations above the mean.

mark_breakdown.desc: Multiplying the probability by total drinks $80$
Rounding to nearest whole number to get 2 drinks

subparts.solution:
$$P(X \ge 254 + 2 \times 2.3) = P(X \ge 258.6) \approx 0.0228$$
$$\therefore \text{we expect about } 0.0228 \times 80 \approx 2 \text{ drinks to have volume at least two standard deviations above the mean.}$$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Expected value of a count is given by $E(Y) = n \times p$, where $p$ is the probability of the specified event.
step_by_step: Find two standard deviations above the mean: $254 + 2(2.3) = 258.6$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting to multiply the probability by the sample size 80 to get the expected number.

subparts.stem: The machine operator guarantees that at least 95% of drinks will have volume at least 250 mL. Is the guarantee valid?

mark_breakdown.desc: Setting up normal distribution calculation for $P(X \ge 250)$ with $\mu = 254$ and $\sigma = 2.3$
Concluding that the operator's guarantee is valid as $0.959 \ge 0.95$

subparts.solution:
$P(X \ge 250) \approx 0.959$

$\therefore$ the operator's guarantee that at least $95\%$ of drinks will have volume at least $250\text{ mL}$ is valid.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The normal cumulative distribution function is used to calculate the probability of a continuous random variable lying above a certain threshold.
step_by_step: Calculate $P(X \ge 250)$ using a normal CDF function with lower bound $250$ and upper bound $\infty$.
Compare the resulting probability $0.959$ ($95.9\%$) to the guaranteed threshold of $95\%$, confirming validity.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Using the variance instead of standard deviation in the calculator.

subparts.stem: A technician adjusts the machine so the standard deviation is now 2.5 mL. What effect does this have on the operator's guarantee?

mark_breakdown.desc: Setting up normal distribution calculation with new standard deviation $\sigma = 2.5$
Concluding that the guarantee is no longer valid as $94.5\% < 95\%$

subparts.solution:
Suppose $X \sim \text{N}(254, (2.5)^2)$.

$P(X \ge 250) \approx 0.945$

$\therefore$ about $94.5\%$ of drinks will have volume at least $250\text{ mL}$.

So, the operator's guarantee is no longer valid.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Changes in standard deviation alter the spread of the distribution, affecting tail probabilities.
step_by_step: Observe that $94.5\%$ is strictly less than the promised $95\%$, hence the guarantee fails.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting to draw the comparison conclusion explicitly.
